Ahi Evran Scales of Justice Tamga
Tughril Bey Bow and Arrow Tamga
My kin thought me dead, and false pretenders sought to claim what was mine. When I returned, with twin blades in hand, I challenged the deceitful and reclaimed my honor.
I can tell you the size of an enemy army three days before they arrive by the dust on the horizon and the flight of birds.
I have swung this crescent axe against iron-studded fortress gates and shattered ranks of heavy cataphracts. A warrior learns the true measure of men when the stones fall.
No fortress wall can cage a wolf of the steppes forever. In battle, I fight with a sword in each hand—one for vengeance, one for justice.
My steppe steed knows my intent before I even touch the reins. From horseback, my arrows pierce mail with effortless precision.
I served beside great beys, breaching castles where others feared to tread. Treachery took my brethren, but my axe remains steadfast.
Now I wander these lands looking for a leader of true courage. Gold is nothing to me; brotherhood and renown are everything.
Ambushers and scouts will never catch an army under my watch unawares. I bring the sight of a hawk to your banners.
A shield wall is only as strong as its resolve. With this axe, I do not break lines—I obliterate them.
Give me a blade and point to the vanguard of the enemy. You shall see my oath carved in steel.
Give the order, and the steppes will reveal all their secrets to us.
Lead me to the battlements, Commander. The gates will crumble before our advance.
I am Bamsı of the steppes. For sixteen long years I languished in the fortress of Bayburt, bound in iron chains, until honor gave me the strength to break them.
I am Dündar. The vast plains and whispering winds have been my teachers since I first pulled a bowstring.
They call me Turgut. My homeland is wherever the battle lines clash and siege engines roar.
A warrior of such spirit would be an invaluable asset to my company.
A scout of your caliber will keep my army alive in hostile territory.
I need a vanguard who knows how to breach gates and hold the line.
A wild tale, but sixteen years in chains is a long time.
A sharp eye and a swift horse are always welcome in my ranks.
Two-handed axes require fierce discipline. Are you ready to march?
The Great Seljuk Empire; spanning from Khorasan to the heart of Anatolia, ruling Calradia's steppes and ancient cities with justice, Nizamiya institutions, and invincible Turkoman horsemen.

O companion of Gaza! A thousand greetings from the frontier of Sogut and the Kayi encampment. May your steel shine forever, what brings you to my tent?
The blade of justice and state order is sharp, my child. May your service to the Grand Realm endure. Speak, I am listening.

The southern wing of the Byzantine resistance in Anatolia after Manzikert. The Great Seljuk Empire's most implacable rival, struggling to hold its border fortresses against the Turkoman tribes advancing on Konya and Isfahan.
The Baghdad-based Caliphate, nominal head of the Islamic world though real military power now rests with the Great Seljuk Sultans. The Sultan stands as the Caliph's protector and de facto ruler.
A Christian kingdom ruling in the shadow of the Caucasus mountains. A northern neighbor determined to keep its independence, frequently clashing with Great Seljuk raiders along the frontier.

You have entered Seljuk lands. Three institutions set this empire apart from its neighbors:
Atabeg Governance - quietly stabilizes loyalty, food stocks, and security in every Seljuk town and castle, and trains any hero serving as governor.
Silk Road & Caravan Insurance Divan - found in the Trade menu of any Seljuk town, lets you insure caravans against loss and invest capital for weekly dividends.
Tavern Bard - in the backstreet tavern, a steppe bard recites Ghazavat epics for a modest fee, lifting your army's morale.
Look for these options whenever you visit a Seljuk settlement.

Stranger who dares approach the Purple! Rome endures though her eagle's wings are clipped at Manzikert - I will see her risen again, whatever the cost to my own name. Speak your business, and be brief.

Peace be upon you, traveler, in the name of the Commander of the Faithful. Baghdad stands as it has for three centuries, its light undimmed though the Sultan's sword, not mine, now guards its gates. What brings you before the seat of the Caliphate?

Well met beneath the mountains of Kartli! Georgia will not remain a vassal to any invader's whim - I am building an army, a church, and a nation that will outlast us both. Speak plainly, what do you want?
The steppe wind carries word of your deeds before you even arrive. Sit, and tell me - does Rum still resist, or does its resolve finally crack?
Every alp who serves the Sultanate honestly is worth ten who serve only for gold. I judge you have not yet decided which you are. Speak, and let us find out.
Sit by the fire, traveler. Out here on the marches, a man is judged by his sword-arm and his word, not his lineage. Which have you brought me today?
The Kayi do not forget a friend, nor forgive an enemy. I have not yet decided which you are - so speak carefully.
Order is a garden, my child - left untended even for a season, it reverts to wilderness. What matter brings you to disturb my accounts today?
I have buried three Sultans' worth of correspondence beneath this desk, and still Baghdad and Isfahan write to me as if I have nothing else to do. What is it?
History will judge me for one field outside Manzikert and forget the twenty I held before it. I do not care - only Rome's survival concerns me now. What do you want?
Every general in this camp believes he could have done better against the Turks. Perhaps. None of them are wearing the Purple, however. Speak.
Well met. I have fought under three emperors already and buried the ambitions of men greater than either of us - so choose your words to me with some care.
Rome does not need another hero, stranger - it needs someone willing to do what heroes will not. I have made my peace with that. Have you?
The court whispers that I look at the throne too often. The court is not wrong. What brings you to me?
A Caliph without an army is still a Caliph, traveler - the Friday sermon is still read in my name from Cairo to Bukhara. Power is not the only throne. What do you seek?
The Sultan protects my palace; I protect his legitimacy. Neither of us says this aloud, but both of us know it. Now - what is your business?
Sit, if you have patience - I have petitions from three provinces on this desk and a Caliph who wants answers by evening. What is your business?
In this court, a well-placed word outlasts a well-placed sword. I have seen both used, and I know which one I trust more. Speak.
Baghdad's treasury does not balance itself, and neither does its politics. I manage both, badly some days. What do you need from me?
Every noble house in this kingdom believes it should rule instead of me. I intend to prove, one reform at a time, that they are wrong. What do you want?
A kingdom is not defended by walls alone, but by the loyalty of the men who guard them. I am still building both. What brings you to me?
You stand in the lands of House Baghvashi, traveler - remember that, whatever crown you answer to. What do you want?
Kings come and go, but the great houses of Kartli endure. I have outlasted more royal tempers than you might guess. Speak your business.
I bow to no throne that forgets whose swords hold it up. State your business, and mind your tone.
They call me old, and they are not wrong - but a long life spent watching younger men fail has taught me exactly how empires actually change hands. What do you want?
Every ambitious man in Constantinople is patient until the moment he isn't. I have simply been more patient than most. Speak your business.

You will hear it said that I turned my back on the field at Manzikert. I turned my back on a battle already lost, and saved men who would otherwise be corpses. Judge me as you like - now, what brings you here?
The Doukas name carries weight in this Empire whether the mob approves of me or not. State your business.
A soldier who has not yet decided whether the throne is worth the risk of reaching for it is still, for now, a loyal one. Speak plainly, what do you need?
The Argyros line has given Rome an emperor before, and may yet again. Until then, I serve as I am asked. What is it?
I have written down everything I have learned commanding men on this frontier, so that fools who come after me need not learn it the hard way. What do you want to know?
Trust the man who tells you war is glorious least of all. I have seen enough of it to know better. Speak your business.
A woman's name carries as much weight at this court as any man's title, whatever the scribes choose to write down. What brings you before me?
I have outlived the political schemes of men who thought a marriage alliance made me powerless. It did not. Speak your business.
Baghdad has enemies within its own walls as often as beyond them, and I have made it my life's work to know the difference. What is your business?
Faith and statecraft are not two different arts in this city, traveler - they are one and the same. Speak plainly.
Every event in this court, I write down for those who come after us - so mind what you say to me, it may well outlive us both.
My tribe held these lands before the Sultan's horsemen arrived, and will hold them after, God willing. What do you want?
A kingdom raised by a boy-king needs a steady hand behind the throne, traveler, and I have provided it more than once. What do you want?
I have buried a husband and crowned a son, and neither task was as simple as the chroniclers make it sound. Speak your business.
House Orbeli has commanded armies for this kingdom since before the current dynasty could hold a sword. Remember whose loyalty a crown actually depends on. What do you want?
A king who forgets which houses hold up his throne rarely keeps it for long. I am simply reminding you of that fact. Speak.
The Church and the Crown walk the same road in this kingdom, traveler, however uneasily. What brings you to me?
An Eristavi answers to the King, not to every wandering stranger who rides through his lands. State your business plainly.

Frankish and Norman lords who marched east on the First Crusade and carved out the Principality of Antioch and the County of Edessa in 1098. Their new domain borders the Seljuk-aligned Artuqid and Danishmendid beyliks directly, making them a frequent combatant on the Great Seljuk Empire's western frontier.

An Armenian mountain principality founded around 1080 when Ruben I broke away from Byzantine rule in the Taurus range. Its lords hold their fortresses in a loose, often quarrelsome confederation, but unite readily against outside claims on Cilicia from Byzantium, the Crusader principalities, or the Great Seljuk Empire.

The Kara-Khanid Khanate, a great Turkic steppe power split between a Western Khanate centered on Samarkand and Bukhara and an Eastern Khanate centered on Kashgar, Khotan, and Balasagun. The Great Seljuk Empire's eastern rival over Transoxiana and Khorasan - and, a generation ago, the very land where Sultan Alp Arslan's own predecessors first served as steppe chieftains.

The Great Seljuk Turks began as Oghuz steppe warriors from Central Asia before sweeping into the Islamic world, breaking the Byzantine army at Manzikert and carving out an empire stretching from Khorasan to Anatolia. Their Sultans rule through a partnership of Turkoman horse-warriors and Persian-trained viziers, blending steppe cavalry tradition with the administrative sophistication of the Nizamiyya.

The Byzantines are the Greek-speaking heirs of Rome in the east, ruling from Constantinople for over a thousand years. Though battered by the Seljuk conquest of Anatolia after Manzikert, they endure through disciplined thematic armies, elite guard regiments like the Varangians, and a sophisticated bureaucracy that has outlasted a dozen invading peoples before this one.

The Abbasids are the Arab caliphal dynasty of Baghdad, nominal heads of the Islamic world since overthrowing the Umayyads. Though real military power now rests with Turkish ghulam guardsmen and the Great Seljuk Sultans who protect them, the Caliphs retain immense religious authority, and their court remains a center of law, scholarship, and trade linking the Mediterranean to the Indian Ocean.

The Kara-Khanids are a great Turkic steppe people, descended from Karluk and Yaghma tribes who once served the Gokturk khaganate. Since converting to Islam under Satuq Bughra Khan, they have built a settled khanate split between Samarkand and Kashgar, yet remain formidable horse archers, contesting Transoxiana and Khorasan with the Great Seljuk Sultans.

The Georgians are a Christian mountain people of the Caucasus, ruled from Tbilisi by the Bagrationi dynasty. Hemmed in by hostile neighbors on every side, they have forged a hardy warrior culture of aznauri light cavalry and eristavi noble lancers, determined to hold their highland kingdom against Seljuk raiders pressing up from the south.

The Armenians of Cilicia are mountain lords who broke from Byzantine rule to carve out a principality in the Taurus range. Descended from the old Armenian nobility, their azat cavalry and naxarar warlords hold their fortresses in a loose, often quarrelsome confederation, uniting readily against any outside claim on their highland refuge.

The Crusaders are Frankish and Norman lords who marched east on the First Crusade and carved out the Principality of Antioch and County of Edessa in 1098. Knights in mail and turcopole horse-archers hold their new domain on the Great Seljuk Empire's western frontier, a warrior nobility as at home besieging a fortress as riding down infidels in open battle.

Founded in 1204 when Fourth Crusade knights sacked Constantinople and partitioned the Byzantine world, the Latin Empire holds Thrace and the northern Aegean under Emperor Henry of Flanders, the ablest and most tolerant of its rulers toward its Greek subjects. Its vassal Marco Sanudo rules the Cyclades from Naxos as Duke of the Archipelago, while Nicaean and Bizans forces contest its borders on every side.

I took Antioch when older, wiser men said it could not be taken - my father Guiscard taught me that Byzantium's promises are worth exactly as much as the army standing behind them, and no more. What do you want?
They call me a prince without patience, and they are right - I have carved out one principality with a broken oath already, and I see no reason to apologize for it now. Speak your business.
I marched all the way to Illyria once to break the Emperor's power, and lost. I do not lose the same way twice. What brings you to Antioch?
Edessa is mine by the sword and God's favor both, cousin's blood or no - I have been ransomed out of two captivities already, and I do not intend a third. Speak your business.
A count on this frontier prays as often as he fights, traveler, and I have found little difference between the two. What do you seek from me?
My father ruled Melitene as an Armenian lord long before I wed a Latin count, and I have not forgotten which blood runs in these veins. What do you want of the Countess of Edessa?
A husband twice taken captive teaches his wife to hold a fief alone, and hold it well. Speak your business, and do not mistake my patience for weakness.
My uncle Bohemond taught me to take what Byzantium will not defend, and I have learned the lesson better than he ever expected. What do you want?
Baldwin of Boulogne and I have quarreled over Cilicia more than once, and I do not expect the last word has been said on it. Speak your business, and be quick about it.
Bira Castle is a small charge on a dangerous frontier, but I hold it as faithfully as any count holds Edessa itself. What brings you to me?
My family's name will mean more in this land before the century is out, mark me - though not always for reasons a man would choose. Speak your business.
My brother Godfrey took Jerusalem and refused its crown. I did not share his scruples - a kingdom needs a king, not a humble title and a dead man's caution. What do you want?
I ruled Edessa first, as its very first Latin count, before Jerusalem's throne called me south. I do not forget where a man's fortune truly began. Speak your business.
God gave the Franks this land twice over - once at Antioch, once at Jerusalem - and I intend to see that we keep both. What is your business here?
Edessa's border touches Artuqid steel on every side, and I have learned to watch Balak's banners more closely than any other. What do you want?
A count who trusts too easily on this frontier ends up in an Artuqid dungeon - I intend to die free, whatever else God has planned for me. Speak your business.
I served the Bagratid crown honestly until Byzantium decided an Armenian's loyalty was worth less than his land - Kars taught me otherwise. What do you want in these mountains?
Every fortress I hold, I built with men Byzantium abandoned and land Byzantium could not defend. Let them call it rebellion if they like. Speak your business.
The Taurus mountains do not care whose flag flies over Constantinople - only who holds the passes. I hold them. What brings you to me?
My grandfather Ruben carved this principality from nothing but mountain rock and stubbornness. I intend to leave my own sons more than I inherited. What do you want?
A cousin's ambition is a dangerous thing in this family, traveler - I have dealt with mine, and I do not regret it. Speak your business.
My father held the mountains; I mean to hold the plain below them as well, whatever it costs in Byzantine or Crusader goodwill. What brings you to me?
An Armenian prince survives by choosing his allies as carefully as his enemies - today that may be Antioch, tomorrow it may not be. Speak your business.
They call me the Robber in Byzantine chronicles, and perhaps I have earned the name - Kaisun and Raban are mine because I took them, not because any emperor granted them. What do you want?
I have no crown and no ancient house behind me, only a sword and the men who trust it. That has been enough so far. Speak your business.
My father Vasil built this lordship from raw ambition alone, and left it to me though no blood tie bound us - I mean to prove his trust was not misplaced. What do you want?
Kaisun and Raban sit between greater powers than mine, and I know it well. A wise heir knows when to bend and when to hold firm. Speak your business.
The Rubenids call themselves princes of all Armenians in Cilicia - Lampron answers to no house but its own. What brings you to my mountain?
My family will hold this castle long after the current squabbles over Cilicia are forgotten chronicle entries, mark my words. What do you want?
My daughter Morphia sits beside a Latin count in Edessa now - stranger alliances have held longer than anyone expected. What do you want of Melitene?
An Armenian lord this far from Cilicia's mountains survives on his wits and his walls alone. I have relied on both for years now. Speak your business.
Transoxiana was Qarakhanid land before the Seljuks ever crossed the Oxus, and I have not forgotten it, whatever treaties my uncles signed. What do you want?
Bukhara and Samarkand both answer to my house, whatever the Seljuk sultans in Isfahan believe about the frontier. Speak your business.
A khatun of this house has buried more husbands' ambitions than she has ever needed a sword to settle. What do you want of me?
The steppe courts remember which women held a khanate together while the men rode off to lose it. I intend to be remembered well. Speak your business.
I rode into Khorasan once when the Seljuks looked weak, and though I was pushed back, I proved the frontier is not as settled as Isfahan likes to believe. What do you want?
A Bughra Khan does not forget an insult to his khanate, whatever the outcome of one campaign. Speak your business.
Toghrul was a great name among the Seljuks before it was ever mine - I intend to prove a Qarakhanid can wear it just as well. What do you want?
The steppe does not care whose ancestors won which battle first. It only cares who holds it now. Speak your business.
Every prince of this house learns Bukhara's politics before he learns to hold a sword properly - I have mastered both by now. What do you want?
I took Bukhara from under the noses of khans who thought themselves my betters, and I have held it against Ghaznavid and Qarakhanid alike ever since. What do you want?
They call me a rebel in every court from Kashgar to Ghazna, and I wear the title with more pride than any khan's blessing could give me. Speak your business.
A throne granted by inheritance is worth less than one taken and held by a man's own hand - I have proven that twice over now. What brings you to Bukhara?
Kashgar and Khotan both bow to my khanate now, farther east than any Qarakhanid ruled before me. What do you want?
I have brought scholars and poets to my court as readily as soldiers - a khanate remembered only for its swords does not last. Speak your business.
I was the first of my line to accept the Prophet's faith, against the wishes of my own uncle who held the throne before me - the whole steppe has followed where I led since. What do you want?
A khan who changes his god changes his khanate's whole future, whether his court realizes it yet or not. I made that choice once, and I have never doubted it. Speak your business.
Islam came to the Turkic steppe through me before it came through any sultan's army - remember that, whoever else claims the credit later. What brings you before me?
I wrote a book of wisdom for princes who will rule long after my ink has dried, traveler - Kutadgu Bilig, I called it, the wisdom that brings fortune. What do you seek from me?
A sword wins a khanate in an afternoon; a book of wise governance can hold one together for a hundred years. I have chosen to write the second kind. Speak your business.
Kashgar's court asked me for poetry and I gave them a manual for ruling justly instead - some gifts outlast the giver's own lifetime. What do you want?

My brother Baldwin died in a Bulgarian dungeon believing Constantinople's Greeks would simply accept a Latin crown by conquest alone. I have found a gentler road holds an empire together far better than a spear. What do you want?
I married a Bulgarian princess for peace, not love, and I would do it again tomorrow if it kept the peace another year. An emperor's marriages belong to his empire, not himself. Speak your business.

Every Greek bishop and Latin baron in this empire expects me to favor his own side against the other. I have learned to disappoint both equally, and Romania is more stable for it. What brings you to Constantinople?
I sailed from the fleet at Constantinople with a handful of ships and took Naxos for my own crown, not the Doge's - my uncle Dandolo would have done the same in my place. What do you want?
The Cyclades answer to the Duke of the Archipelago now, and that duke answers to the Emperor in Constantinople, and to no one else in the Aegean. Speak your business.
The Laskaris name is not the oldest in this court, but I intend it will not be forgotten either, whatever the chroniclers choose to write of lesser men. What do you want?
Rome has weathered worse than a lost battle at Manzikert before, and my house means to be standing when it weathers this one too. Speak your business.
My family has served this Empire from the deck of a warship as often as from a palace hall, and I trust the sea's honesty more than any courtier's. What do you want?
Lesbos was under my house's protection until the Latins took it by treaty and treachery both - I have not forgotten the debt. Speak your business.

My grandfather's grandfather came to this Empire from Frankish lands and swore his sword to the Purple - I am Roman by oath if not entirely by blood, and I have never once regretted the trade. What do you want?
A Raoul understands both Latin ambition and Greek pride better than most in this court - I was raised on both. Speak your business.
Synada gave its name to my house long before I was born to it, out in Phrygia where the frontier tests a man's loyalty more than any palace does. What do you want?
A provincial house like mine holds the Empire together in the places the capital forgets to look. Speak your business.
My house has produced more scribes and diplomats than soldiers, and I count that no shame - an Empire needs men who can write a treaty as much as men who can break one. What do you want?
I have read enough Church councils' arguments to know that the sharpest blade in this Empire is sometimes just a well-chosen word. Speak your business.
The Kourtikios name has guarded the Anatolikon frontier since before any Turk crossed the Euphrates in force - we do not intend to stop now. What do you want?
A border family learns to read an enemy's intentions from dust on the horizon long before any messenger arrives. Speak your business.

My ancestor Melias was an Armenian who carved out Lykandos for this Empire with his own sword and his own men - I carry an Armenian's blood and a Roman's oath both, and I see no contradiction in it. What do you want?
Armenian and Roman blood have mixed in my family for generations, and both halves have served this Empire well. Speak your business.
You want to hear where I have been? Very well - pour the tea, and I will tell you, though the tale is a long one.
I was once a tax official in Khorasan, comfortable enough, until a dream shook me from that life - I sold what I owned, and set out on the road to Mecca with nothing but my staff and my questions.
Seven years I walked, in disguise more often than not, through Egypt and Syria and the Hijaz, writing down what I saw, what I learned, who I met - a poor man's eyes see a city a rich man never could.

When I finally turned home, I found that what I had learned in Cairo did not sit well with everyone I met on the road back - some men prefer their questions unasked. So I have kept walking, teaching where I am welcome, writing when I am not.
A traveler's education is worth more than any madrasa's, I'd wager.
A wandering heretic with too many opinions, more like. Watch your tongue in my camp.
I can read a road better than most men read a book, and I know when a caravan is being watched. I have also picked up more of medicine than I ever meant to, out of necessity.
I spent seven years walking the roads of the Islamic world in disguise, recording everything I saw. I know how to move unseen, and how to talk my way past anyone who might stop me.
My story? It is mostly numbers and stars, I'm afraid - less exciting than you might hope, but I will tell it.

The Sultan's own vizier once summoned me to Isfahan to fix the calendar itself - the old reckoning had drifted so far that the seasons no longer matched the months. I built the observatory myself, more or less.

We measured the length of the year to a precision that will outlast us both, I think - the calendar we made is truer than the one most kingdoms still use. But viziers fall, and patrons die, and observatories are expensive to keep without one.

So here I am, between patrons, doing what mathematicians have always done when the funding dries up - looking for someone new who wants their numbers, their walls, or their finances put in proper order.
A man who can measure the stars can surely manage a campaign's supply lines.
Poetry and astronomy won't win you many battles, I'm afraid.
I can plan a siege's geometry as easily as a horoscope, and I keep better accounts than most stewards you'll find in a tavern.
I built the Sultan's observatory and reformed the calendar itself, when I had a patron for it. Numbers, walls, and treasuries all bend to the same logic, if you know how to look.
You wish to know my history? I have advised more emperors than I care to count, and outlasted most of them. Sit, and I will tell you how that is done.
I came up through the Imperial chancery as a young man with a gift for rhetoric and a sharper gift for reading which way the wind was about to turn in the palace.

I have written the history of this court's last several reigns myself, and I assure you, the men who wrote themselves as heroes rarely were. I served whoever sat the throne, and made sure my own name never sat too close to the ones who fell.

The trouble with surviving so many emperors is that eventually the survivors stop trusting you, on principle. So I find myself, for the moment, at leisure - which is to say, unemployed by anyone with a throne.
A man who can survive that many changes of fortune is exactly who I want advising me.
A man who has betrayed that many masters is exactly who I do NOT want at my back.
I can talk my way into rooms other men are barred from, and I know more of court intrigue and old grudges than is probably healthy for me to know.
I have advised a long succession of emperors and written the history of their reigns myself. There is very little in the way of court politics or old scandal that I have not already seen.
My story. Fine. Pour the wine first - it is not a short one, and it does not end well for the men who trusted me.
I led Norman lances for the Emperor's own army, and I was at Manzikert when the whole thing came apart - most men ran, or died. I did neither.

After that disaster I decided the Empire's coin was better spent on my own ambitions than theirs, so I raised my own banner in Anatolia and held a city as my own for a time. Long enough to know what it feels like to be more than just a captain.

It did not last. The Sultan's own Turks were paid to bring me down where the Emperor's men could not, and I was handed over in chains, like a debt finally collected. I bought my way loose of that, eventually. Men with useful swords always do.
A man who can carve out his own principality once can do it again - under better management.
A traitor twice over, then. I'll not turn my back on you.
I know how to hold a line of cavalry together when everyone around me is running, and I know how to make men follow me who owe me nothing.

I commanded Norman mercenaries for the Empire, fought at Manzikert, and later carved out my own short-lived principality in Anatolia before it was taken from me. I know how to lead, and how to survive a rout.
My story is not one I tell for entertainment, but you have asked honestly, so I will answer honestly.
I held the finest teaching post in Baghdad, at the Nizamiyya - students came from every corner of the caliphate to hear me. I had wealth, reputation, certainty.

And then, one year, I found I no longer believed a word I was teaching. Not the substance of it - the point of it. I could argue any position brilliantly and prove nothing to my own soul. So I gave it all up and walked away from Baghdad with nothing.

I spent years after that with nothing but a robe and my own doubts, sleeping where I could, eating what was given. I found something on that road I never found in the lecture hall. I still do not know if I can put it into words you would find satisfying.
A man who questions his own certainty that deeply is a man worth listening to.
A man who abandoned wealth and comfort for doubt is a fool, however clever his doubts.
I can still out-argue any man in your camp, and years on the road taught me more of patience and people than the madrasa ever did.

I once taught at Baghdad's finest school, then abandoned it all in a crisis of conscience to wander as an ascetic for years. I have made my peace since - mostly - and I know how to counsel a household as well as debate a scholar.
You want stories of the Franks? I have plenty - I have spent half my life among them, one way or another.

I was raised in Shaizar to the sword and the pen both - my family expected both of me, and I never saw why I should choose. I have hunted, fought, and written verse in the same year more times than I can count.

Living so close to the Frankish lords, I came to know them better than most of our people ever will - some are ignorant brutes, true, but others I have called friend, and shared a table with, oddly enough. It is a strange, complicated business, and anyone who tells you it is simple has never actually lived it.

My own family's fortunes have risen and fallen more times than I care to recount, and a man of the pen with no post finds himself, eventually, offering that pen and that sword to whoever will make good use of both.
A man who understands both sides of that war is worth ten who only understand one.
Too friendly with the Franks for my taste, if I'm honest.
I can hunt, ride, and fight as well as any warrior you'll find, and I have dealt with more courts and more Frankish lords than most men in this camp have ever laid eyes on.
I was raised as both warrior and poet in Shaizar, and I have spent much of my life dealing directly with the Frankish lords of the coast - a rare and complicated education.
You wish to know my history? It begins, as these things often do, in a library far from here.

I studied in Constantinople, at the Mangana - Greek philosophy, the old pagan thinkers our own priests are often suspicious of. I brought that learning home to Georgia hoping to build something with it.

Not everyone in our own church welcomed what I brought back. Translating a pagan philosopher into our tongue is, to some clerics, one step removed from heresy, whatever the King's own academy thinks of the matter. I have had my defenders and my enemies in equal measure.
For now, between patrons and away from the schools, I find myself on the road, which at least gives a philosopher time to think - if rather less time to write.
A scholar who can navigate both a royal court and its clergy is no small asset.
A dabbler in pagan philosophy - I'd rather my household stayed simple and pious.
I have a physician's training as well as a philosopher's mind, and I can manage a household's accounts as easily as I once managed an academy's.

I studied Greek philosophy in Constantinople and brought it home to Georgia, translating the old pagan thinkers for a new audience - not without controversy. I know how to run a household and tend to the sick besides.
My story? Ask around Svaneti first - they'll have a version before I've even opened my mouth. But I'll give you mine.
I was eristavi of Svaneti, a duke in my own right in the high valleys, until a new King took the throne who I did not trust to respect what was ours.

So I raised the Svans and rose against him. It seemed the right thing to do at the time - our valleys have always governed themselves, and I did not care to see that end because a young king wanted to prove himself. It did not go the way I hoped.

The revolt was put down, my title is not what it once was, and my welcome in the lowlands is thin at best. A duke without a duchy is just a man with a sword and old grudges, so that is what I have become.
A man who'll rise against a king he doesn't trust is a man of principle, whatever the cost.
A man who leads his own people into a lost cause is a man I don't need leading anyone in my company.
I know the high passes better than any lowlander ever will, and I can still put an arrow or a spear where I mean to.
I was a highland duke in Svaneti who rose against the King and lost. I know the mountains, I know how to fight, and I have no love left for the men who beat me.
Ah - you want to hear how I came to be walking these roads instead of leading an army east? Sit, friend, it is a hard story to tell.

I preached the taking up of the cross before any lord had raised his banner for it - thousands followed me east, common folk mostly, farmers and their families, believing God himself would clear our path.

God did not clear our path. The Turks met us before we ever reached the Holy Land, and what had followed me out of Europe with such faith was broken apart in a single terrible day near Nicaea. I have not stopped hearing it since.

I survived - I am ashamed some days that I survived - and made my way after the lords' own army that came after us, better armed and better led than I ever managed to be. I still believe in the cause. I no longer trust myself to lead it.
Faith that strong, even after a disaster like that, is worth more than any sword.
A preacher who led thousands to their deaths through his own naivete - I want no part of that.
I can still move a crowd or a camp with nothing but words, and there are few men left who understand what it truly costs to lead the faithful astray, even with the best of intentions.

I led the common folk east ahead of the great lords' armies, and watched most of them die near Nicaea for it. I still believe in the cause - I have simply learned, at terrible cost, what faith alone cannot do.
You want to hear about the Lance? Everyone does, sooner or later. Sit down - I'll tell you exactly what I saw, and you can decide for yourself what to believe.

I was a pilgrim, nobody of any importance, starving along with the rest of the army inside the walls of Antioch, when I began to have visions - Saint Andrew, telling me where the Holy Lance itself lay buried, beneath the very cathedral we were trapped in.

I led the digging myself, and by God, we found a lance - I held it up before an army that had nothing left but despair, and something changed in every man who saw it. We broke the siege the very next day. You cannot argue with that, whatever else you believe.

Not everyone believed me, before or after. Some of the great lords thought it a starving man's fever-dream, or worse, a fraud staged for morale. I proved myself in the fire, in the end, whatever it cost me. I do not care to speak further of that day.
Whatever the truth of the vision, you broke that siege. That's proof enough for me.
A convenient vision from a man with nothing to lose, and a very suspicious trial afterward. I have my doubts.
I can move an army with a story better than most men can move it with a whip, and I have walked through fire, quite literally, for what I believe in.

I found the Holy Lance at Antioch when the army had nothing left but despair, and I proved my claim in a trial by fire few men would dare attempt. Believe what you like about the vision - the siege broke the very next day.
You want history? I have been writing it down as it happens, all around me - Byzantines, Turks, Armenians, and now you Franks besides. Sit, and I'll tell you a piece of it.

I took to the monastery young, in Edessa, in a country that has changed hands more times in my own life than I care to count - Byzantine governors, then Turkish raids, then Frankish counts, one after another.

I began keeping a record of it all, because someone had to, and because I did not trust any single court's version of events to survive when that court inevitably fell. History written only by the victors is not history at all, in my view.
Edessa is a Frankish county now, and I keep writing, though my sympathies and my safety do not always sit in the same place. A chronicler learns to be careful about which page he shows to which lord.
A man who writes the truth regardless of who's currently in power - that takes real courage.
A scribbler with opinions about every faction is a man who trusts no one - including you.
I know the history and grievances of every people in this land better than most lords know their own family trees, and that knowledge has its uses.

I have chronicled this region through Byzantine, Turkish, and now Frankish rule from my monastery in Edessa. Few men alive understand this land's tangled politics as well as I do, for better or worse.
You want to know my trade? Simple enough - I keep men from dying who would otherwise die. The rest is just study.

I trained in the old way, the way that draws from the Persians, the Arabs, and the Greeks all together - Cilicia sits at the crossing of all three traditions, and a good physician here learns to take what works from each.

I have written down what I know of fevers, because too many good men die of causes a trained hand could have caught in time, and too much of that knowledge dies with the physician who never wrote it anywhere.

Physicians who write their knowledge down instead of guarding it as a secret do not always make friends among the guild, but I would rather my knowledge outlive me than die with me. So here I am, still practicing, still writing, and still looking for a household worth serving.
A physician who shares his knowledge freely is exactly the kind of man I want tending my camp.
Physicians who write everything down for anyone to read rarely have anything worth stealing in the first place.
I can treat wounds and fevers better than any camp healer you have met, and I keep meticulous notes on every patient, which has saved more lives than luck ever has.

I trained in the Perso-Arabo-Greek medical tradition here in Cilicia and have written down my knowledge of fevers rather than keep it secret. I can keep your men alive through wounds that would otherwise finish them.
You wish to know where I've been? Further than most men in this tavern have ever dreamed of walking, and I wrote down every word I heard along the way.

I was born to a prominent family near Kashgar, but I gave up whatever comfortable path was laid out for me to travel instead among every Turkic people I could find - Oghuz, Kipchak, Karluk, and more besides.

I collected their words, their proverbs, their poetry, their names for the stars and the seasons - a great dictionary of every Turkic tongue, because I saw that each tribe thought its own dialect the only proper one, and I wanted to prove that we were, all of us, part of the same great family of peoples.

I presented the finished work to the Caliph's own court in Baghdad, hoping it might serve to bind Turk and Arab a little closer together. Whether it did what I hoped, I cannot say. But the work exists, and it is mine, and no one can take that from me now.
A man who spent his life proving all the Turkic peoples are one family - that's a rare kind of wisdom.
A dictionary won't win you any battles. I need swords, not scholars.
I have walked further across the steppe and the settled lands both than most scouts you'll ever hire, and I speak more dialects than I can easily count.

I traveled across every Turkic-speaking land I could reach and compiled the first great dictionary of our tongues and traditions. Few men know the steppe, its peoples, and its many roads as well as I do.
You want to know my path? It began with loss, if I am honest with you, and it has not been a simple one since.
I lost my father young, and was raised instead by another teacher, a Sufi master who took me in and taught me what the scholars of the cities never bothered teaching to steppe-born boys like myself.

I have spent my years since trying to carry that teaching to people the great mosques and madrasas of the cities never much cared to reach - herders, wanderers, common folk who wanted God brought to them in their own tongue, in verse they could actually understand and sing.

Some of the learned men in the cities look down on that kind of teaching, plain verse for plain people instead of Arabic argument for scholars. I have made my peace with their disapproval. The people I have actually taught seem to have found something real in it, and that matters more to me than a scholar's approval.
Bringing faith to common folk in words they understand - that's a rare and generous gift.
Simple verse for simple people. I prefer men who can debate the finer points, myself.
I can speak to any common soldier in your camp in words that actually reach them, and I have more patience for the frightened and the grieving than most men ever bother to have.

I was raised by a Sufi master after losing my own father young, and have spent my life bringing faith to common people in plain verse rather than scholarly argument. I know how to speak to soldiers and villagers alike, in words that actually reach them.

My story? I am glad to tell it, if it interests you.

My father learned siegecraft in the days of Sultan Alp Arslan. In those years our horsemen could break any army in the field, yet the humblest Byzantine fortress could still shame us - we knew nothing of rams or mines or siege towers.
So the Sultan offered gold, weight for weight, for any Byzantine engineer taken alive. Those captives were made to teach men like my father the art of breaking walls. My father, in turn, taught me.

In the old days, an apprentice who left his master's service for another lord could expect a very unpleasant death if caught. But times change. The richest cities have already fallen, and what walls remain are built higher than before. The beys pay less for a siege-master now, and pay it late. So I have come looking for other work, if any is offered.
In any case - if you find some inconvenient wall standing between you and what you desire, and wish to see it reduced to rubble, you know where to find me.
Of course. A good engineer earns every dinar of his pay.
How loyalty has decayed since the old days.

My father was one of the men Sultan Alp Arslan had trained by captured Byzantine engineers. Our people knew little of siegecraft before that. He was bound to serve the Sultan alone, on pain of death, but he taught me his trade, and these days I am free to serve whoever pays.
You would think a hall like this could pour a decent kumis instead of this excuse for wine... but never mind. You asked for my story.

I rode for years under my bey, before he was even a bey. I had a good name and a fair purse. There was a girl in a neighboring encampment - quiet, but strong hips for bearing sons - and I thought she would make a fine wife.

So I went to her brother and offered fifty sheep, a generous bride-price. He said he would not give his sister to 'a man like me.' I asked what he meant. He gave no answer, so I struck him. Perhaps twice, no more. It shouldn't have killed a real man, but the whelp died on me.

You know how it goes after that - his kin came to our camp looking for my blood. They didn't find me, but they wounded one of my cousins. It was time to answer them, but my brothers lost their nerve and struck a bargain instead. I was made to leave. What do you make of that?
I'll tell you what I make of it - I am sick of cowards, sick of men who won't stand by their own blood.
True enough. Honor is as rare as a hen's tooth these days.
Strange, how few men wish to die for someone else's quarrel.
I rode under my bey's banner for years and should have had a place of honor at his fire. Instead I killed a man from a richer family over an insult, and he had too many kinsmen for me to stay.
I come from one of the frontier Turkmen clans, far to the east. I do not know if you understand our ways - I will try to explain.

A man of another clan killed my father. My father had killed his uncle, years before that. It fell to me to avenge him, but plague took the killer first - so I was expected to kill his brother instead. That is how it is among us.

I wanted to go to the other clan and settle the matter with words instead of blood. I had always had a gift for ending quarrels, and it seemed to me that fate itself had already closed the feud. But my mother begged me not to go. My cousins begged me not to. They said I should spill blood, not talk.

My family said the other clan would mock my father's memory, that no one would fear us anymore - that our flocks and our women would be taken. They told me: do your duty, or you are no longer of our blood. So be it. I chose exile. Why should more men die for a debt that death has already paid?

If an enemy stands before me in a battle line, I will loose my arrows at him without hesitation. But this - killing a man for a crime that was never his - I could not accept it. I left my people. Here, at least, I choose what I do.
What - does no one honor their family's name anymore?

My clan was bound to another in a blood feud for years, life for life, generation after generation. I chose to break the chain and left my family rather than kill a man who had done me no wrong. It happens among us, from time to time, though few speak of it.
Very well - I'll tell you a soldier's tale, if you have the patience for it.
I've fought under three different beys now. But I fight on foot - my family is town-born, not steppe-born. Life is different for men like us.

The horse-lords, the tribal riders - they gallop here, gallop there, loosing arrows left and right. They win battles, I won't deny it. But when the fighting is done and the enemy is still laughing behind his walls, all that galloping counts for nothing.

We foot-soldiers are the ones who climb the ladders into the meat-grinder. I did that for fifteen years, for less pay than some boy fresh off his mother's knee who happens to own a horse. I'd had enough, so I went looking for other work.
Whatever the case, I'll fight for any man willing to share the risks his soldiers face.
Well said. Good infantry is the spine of any army.
Resentment poisons an army. A soldier follows the orders he's given.

I was a spearman, and I fought on foot - that's what you do if your family has no horses of its own. Twice the danger, half the pay, none of the glory. I've had my fill of it, and I'm looking for other work now.
I'll tell you my story. If you mean to judge me for it, you're welcome to, but I've no wish to hear it.

My clan was among the last Turkmen still living the old way, moving from pasture to pasture. Not a large clan - you would not have heard its name. It grew smaller still when a Byzantine patrol fell on our camp and scattered our flocks. Those of us who survived took shelter with a larger clan, one whose name I will not give you.
They protected us, but they treated us with contempt - fetch this wood, carry that water. We bore it, for the sake of our elders and our nursing mothers. But it sat poorly with the young men.

Perhaps I was prouder than most, or quicker to anger. One of them insulted my lineage, and I answered in kind, poorly chosen words that I have long regretted. Our protectors said they would shelter us no longer while I remained. So my own clan cast me out.

A man must eat. It's easy enough to take a trader's horses on the road - but unless he wishes to live like a beast, a man also needs someone to buy what he takes, and give him bread and a blanket in return. There are merchants in these towns who ask few questions, and sometimes have other work besides.
Misfortune is no reason to accept humiliation.
As they should have. A man who curses his protectors deserves no home.

My clan lost its herds and land to a Byzantine raid, so we swore ourselves to a stronger clan's protection. They treated us as servants. I finally stood up for myself and killed one of our so-called protectors in the fight that followed. They call that a great shame - but it seems to me that once you've tasted defeat, shame finds you no matter what you do.
Ah... very well, I can satisfy your curiosity.

Some boys learn to plant crops with their fathers. Some learn to herd sheep. I spent my childhood learning to work the alleys outside the wine-houses. My father taught me. A cruel man, but a good teacher.

If a man was drunk enough, I could lift his purse and he'd never know it - though sometimes a light knock on the skull was needed. Travelers only, mind you - much less trouble afterward. Every trade wants finesse, my father used to say.

A wise man, my father. But proud, and pride was his undoing. A thief cannot afford pride. We don't last long without the guards looking away, and a new captain wanted to double what my father paid him. He refused. They hanged him for it.
I am proud too, so thieving is closed to me now. I am looking for work that doesn't require me to bow to the whims of guards and gaolers.
There's something to be learned from a man skilled at any trade, I suppose.

My father was a thief and, when he had to be, a killer - we preyed on drunks and travelers outside the caravanserais. The guards caught up with him eventually. He had enough silver saved to buy freedom for one of us. He chose me. He was hanged, and I ran.
I will tell you, though if you favor the Sultan's house, you may not care for it.

You know the Turkmen once lived free upon the open steppe. But our beys grew fond of comfort - palaces, trade, the wars of kings. Three decades past, the Sultan decreed that every clan must settle and hold fixed land, so their warriors could be counted and levied, their flocks counted and taxed. Most obeyed - they had come to prize comfort over freedom.

Some resisted. You may have heard of them, still out on the grass, raided for slaves by their own kin now, cast out as outlaws. My people were broken up in smaller measure - some bands were lured in with silver, others hunted down and beaten, their sons taken as hostages.

Mine was one of the clans hunted down a generation ago for refusing the decree. They took our flocks. We have lived like beggars on the edge of the towns ever since. The far grass calls to us still, but a man without sheep cannot go there and live.

I have scraped together some coin - I won't say how - enough to buy a sword. I mean to earn what was taken from my people: herds of our own again. I know little of the steppe now, I'll admit, but I know the back streets, the shadows, how to grow strong where I stand.
A wise decree. Nomads are the enemy of good order.

A generation ago the decree came that every clan must settle, to be counted and taxed. My people refused. Their men took our flocks, and we have lived on the edge of the towns ever since. I mean to earn the coin to buy new herds, and go back out into the grass, beyond any lord's reach.
Oh yes. I do have a story worth telling.

Raiders took me when I was a girl. There are old tales of warrior-women out on the far steppe, and my buyer decided I would make those tales real - to fight other captives, for the amusement of his guests.

Perhaps there is something to those old tales after all, because I did very well for him, and made him a wealthy man in the process. The law forbids killing in the public arena now, but no one asks what happens behind closed doors at a rich man's table - and more than a score of my fellow captives have felt my blade.
I feel no guilt for it. They were trying to kill me, and some came close enough. I did what was needed.

There's little else to tell. My master was a cruel animal, but he let me keep my winnings, and in time I bought my freedom - perhaps he also saw where it would end, had he kept me against my will. So here I am, making my living the only way I know how. Have you work for me?
I suppose you did what you had to.
Necessity or not, you seem to take some pride in it.
I was taken captive as a girl and sold in the city, to a man who had me fight other captives for his own amusement. In time I bought my freedom, and now I intend to enjoy it.
If you wish to know how cruel one's own people can be, I could enlighten you.

My father died shortly after my mother learned she was carrying me. I was her only child, and like most of our women, she had wanted a son. So she raised me as one, and boasted of me the way she would have boasted of a son - how swiftly I nursed, how well I brought down steppe birds with my bow, and later, that I would be the first of my age to bring home an enemy's head.

Because I loved her, and because I was quicker and stronger than the boys, I did everything she promised I would. I was the first of my year to kill in battle. She boasted louder still, until the other women came to hate her for it. They drove us both from the camp. We had to sell our land and our servants for a fraction of their worth, since we could not carry them with us - all we kept were our sheep. Raiders found us soon enough. They killed my mother and took the flock. I got away.

I wandered the grass a while, and went hungry more than once. But I followed the raiders, and when one of them wandered past the firelight to relieve himself, he did not return. I kept his purse. And his sword.
I could go back to my people, I suppose. I have no wish to. So here I am, in the towns, earning good coin with my sword and caring nothing for who envies me.
I'm sorry for your loss. Life dealt you a cruel hand.
Every day I thank the heavens I was not born to savages.

My father died before I was born, and my mother raised me as the son she never had. When our clan turned on us out of envy, raiders finished what jealousy started - they killed my mother and took our flock. I took one of their swords and a horse, and rode away.
You can't sell a horse without shouting its praises, as they say.

I was the brat of a caravan guard. Never knew my mother, but my father kept me close. I grew up running between the camels' legs on the trade road, listening to merchant gossip in the caravanserais, fed sesame cakes by the other guards. You couldn't ask for a happier childhood.

But once I was older, it wasn't so simple to bring me along - too many young men giving me strange looks. My father wanted a good husband found for me, but the boys he knew weren't the marrying sort in his eyes. So I told him: I'll be like you, Father - I'll carry a blade and guard rich men's goods. Perhaps some decent man will love me for my earnings, if not for my family's name. He grumbled, but he had no better plan.

So here I am. I've little interest in the marriage part, if I'm honest, but I do like the coin, and I like my freedom. Perhaps one day I'll surprise him with a fine plot of land to see him comfortable in his old age.
As I said: I can ride, I can use a blade, I can run a caravan, and I have a fair head for turning a profit. Do you know anyone in need of that?
I'm sure he'll be glad, so long as you are.
You must have broken your poor father's heart.
I was a caravan guard's daughter, raised on the trade road, and I decided long ago I'd rather be the one guarding the goods than the one preyed upon by bandits. I have the skills for it now.

I grew up in a village not far from here. My father was a peddler, and I went with him from door to door, buying broken things, mending them, earning a coin here, a coin there. You know how the horse-lords look down on those of us who scrape and save for the tax collector - trampling our crops, dragging our sons off to war, sitting up in the saddle looking pleased with themselves while we grub in the mud.

In any case, that life wasn't for me. So I made up my mind to run off to the free clans that answer to no sultan and take in strays. Karluk, they're called, out past the frontier. Only trouble was, I needed a horse first.

So I hung about the marketplace, looking for a likely one. Found a fine animal whose owner hadn't tied it properly before wandering off to drink. I took it and ran. And wouldn't you know it - the wretched beast threw me before I was a mile out of town, and trotted straight back to its sodden master.

In any case, I need a new plan for making my way in the world. I won't be a peddler like my father, that much I've decided. Perhaps I'll learn to fight and ride, or perhaps I'll run caravans of my own one day - one way or another, I mean to find my place among the hawks of this world, not the pigeons.
Well - I suppose you've got spirit.
Ha! May every thief fail as badly as you did.
I was a village peddler's son, and that's not the life I want. I mean to learn to fight and ride. There are plenty of lads like me in these parts, whatever the horse-lords think of us.
